subject: Miyoshi et al. (1969)
object: Miyoshi et al. (1969) reported familial holotopistic striatal necrosis.

subject: Marsden et al. (1986)
object: Marsden et al. (1986) described 7 members of 2 families with dystonia that was variably associated with subacute visual loss or asymptomatic optic atrophy. CT scans showed striking bilateral symmetrical lucencies, especially in the putamen.

subject: Marsden et al. (1986)
object: Marsden et al. (1986) suggested that the disorder could be a variant of Leigh disease, but noted considerable differences from pathologically proven Leigh disease. They stated that the condition must be excluded in all patients thought to have idiopathic dystonia, subacute visual failure resembling Leber optic neuropathy, or both.

subject: Novotny et al. (1986)
object: Novotny et al. (1986) studied a kindred in which 8 members had the neuroretinopathy of Leber disease, 14 had progressive generalized dystonia attributed to striatal degeneration, and 1 had both disorders.

subject: Novotny et al. (1986)
object: In the kindred studied by Novotny et al. (1986), the mode of inheritance was compatible with maternal transmission. The authors suggested that this neurologic disorder may be a mitochondrial disease.

subject: Jun et al. (1994)
object: Jun et al. (1994) studied a 5-generation Hispanic family in which members had maternally transmitted Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), early-onset dystonia associated with bilateral basal ganglia lesions, or both.

subject: Jun et al. (1994)
object: Jun et al. (1994) found that LHON and/or dystonia in the 5-generation Hispanic family were transmitted maternally.

subject: Jun et al. (1994)
object: Jun et al. (1994) amplified buffy coat mtDNA from a severely affected child by PCR and sequenced more than 90% of it. The mtDNA belonged to Native American haplogroup D and differed from the Cambridge sequence at 40 positions. One of these, a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 14459 in the ND6 gene, changed a moderately conserved alanine to valine at residue 72 (A72V). The variant was absent from 38 Native American haplogroup D mtDNAs and from 108 Asian, 103 Caucasian, and 99 African mtDNAs. All 6 maternal relatives tested, across 3 generations, carried the mutation. One female relative with LHON was heteroplasmic. The authors suggested that this was the disease-causing mutation.

subject: De Vries et al. (1996)
object: De Vries et al. (1996) studied a large Dutch family with a rare form of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) associated with hereditary spastic dystonia. Some family members had both neuropathy and ophthalmologic lesions, while others had only one of the two types of abnormality.

subject: De Vries et al. (1996)
object: In the Dutch family with LHON and dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) found none of the mtDNA mutations previously reported in LHON. Sequencing of the protein-coding mitochondrial genes identified a heteroplasmic A-to-G transition at nucleotide 11696 in the ND4 gene, which resulted in a val312-to-ile substitution.

subject: De Vries et al. (1996)
object: In the same Dutch family, De Vries et al. (1996) also identified a homoplasmic T-to-A transition at nucleotide 14596 in the ND6 gene, which resulted in an ile26-to-met substitution.

subject: De Vries et al. (1996)
object: De Vries et al. (1996) found a severe complex I deficiency in a muscle biopsy from the family. They concluded that this provided a link between the mtDNA mutations and the complex phenotype that included Leber optic neuropathy.

subject: Watanabe et al. (2006)
object: Watanabe et al. (2006) described a Japanese family with generalized dystonia, attributed to striatal degeneration, that began in childhood, together with optic neuropathy of late onset.

subject: Watanabe et al. (2006)
object: Watanabe et al. (2006) sequenced the whole mitochondrial genome of the proband from a Japanese family with LHON and dystonia and found 42 nucleotide changes compared with the revised Cambridge Reference Sequence. One of them was the G14459A mutation in the NADH dehydrogenase subunit 6 gene (MTND6), which was absent in 200 healthy Japanese controls. The authors noted that this mutation had previously been suggested to cause LHON and/or dystonia in Hispanic, African American, and Caucasian families. They stated that this was the first case of LHON with dystonia in which an mtDNA mutation had been found in a Japanese family.

subject: Watanabe et al. (2006)
object: Watanabe et al. (2006) also found an A3203G mtDNA change in the proband. It was absent in 200 healthy Japanese controls, but its significance remained unknown.

subject: Spruijt et al. (2007)
object: Spruijt et al. (2007) reported a family in which Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) and spastic dystonia occurred together. The authors noted that the family's clinical characteristics were similar to those of previously described families with LHON and dystonia carrying an ND6 mutation.

subject: Spruijt et al. (2007)
object: In a patient with LHON from a family with LHON and spastic dystonia who did not carry 1 of the 3 primary LHON mutations, Spruijt et al. (2007) screened the complete mitochondrial DNA and identified a 3697G>A mutation in the ND1 gene. The heteroplasmy level was determined, and the mutation seemed associated with an isolated complex I deficiency. The authors concluded that the mutation causes the LHON and spastic dystonia phenotype in this family, noted that it can also cause MELAS syndrome, and suggested that other genetic factors may contribute to clinical expression.

subject: Spruijt et al. (2007)
object: Spruijt et al. (2007) found that the ND1 3697G>A mutation seemed associated with an isolated complex I deficiency in their family with LHON and spastic dystonia.

subject: Wang et al. (2009)
object: Wang et al. (2009) described a Chinese family with 18 patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and dystonia (LDYT), a mitochondrial disorder associated with variable combinations of vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia.

subject: Wang et al. (2009)
object: In affected members of a Chinese family with LDYT, Wang et al. (2009) identified a homoplasmic m.10197G>A mutation in the MTND3 gene, resulting in an ala47-to-thr substitution at a highly conserved residue, on a haplogroup D4b background. The mutation was found by resequencing microarray analysis of the entire mitochondrial genome, and quantitative analysis showed homoplasmy in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side. This was the first description of an ND3 mutation causing LDYT.

subject: Wang et al. (2009)
object: Wang et al. (2009) noted that the m.10197G>A MTND3 mutation had also been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome, and suggested that the clinical presentations associated with this mutation are wider, encompassing both LDYT and Leigh syndrome.

subject: Wang et al. (2009)
object: Wang et al. (2009) noted that LDYT had previously been attributed to mutations in the mitochondrial ND6 or ND4 genes, and identified MTND3 as an additional causative gene.

subject: LEBER OPTIC ATROPHY AND DYSTONIA
object: Decreased activity of mitochondrial complex I
